passage:
Lavanya's diary, Sunday night.
Went to my neighbour Minakshi's flat today. Her husband's funeral was on Friday, and the living room was full of relatives, all speaking in low voices and nobody sure what to do with their hands. I brought a pot of khichdi because I didn't know what else to bring. Minakshi's mother-in-law kept saying, “Just sit, beta.” So I sat. When one relative began a long story about a cousin's troubles, the room went stiff, and Minakshi's son stared at the wall. I washed the plates without asking. Later, at the door, Minakshi held my hand and said only, “Thank you for coming.” I had no perfect words, and it didn't seem to matter. I'll go on Thursday with lunch and stay an hour.
Lavanya

qa.q: What did Lavanya bring to Minakshi's flat?
qa.a: Lavanya brought a pot of khichdi.

qa.q: What did Lavanya feel about not having perfect words?
qa.a: Lavanya felt unsure and a little helpless at first, and then seemed to be reassured, since Minakshi only said “Thank you for coming” and the missing words did not seem to matter.

qa.q: What did Lavanya choose to do in the room that helped?
qa.a: Lavanya sat when told to, washed the plates without being asked and planned another visit with lunch, offering presence and small practical help, not speeches.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Minakshi's son when the relative told the long story?
qa.a: Minakshi's son may have felt uncomfortable or numb, since the room went stiff and he stared at the wall, and a long story may have made his own loss harder to bear. 🤍

grounding: An adult brings food, shows up, listens and does small practical tasks for a bereaved family, since presence is worth more than perfect words.

passage:
Akash: Saurabh, Meera's father passed away Thursday. The team wants to go on Saturday. I don't know what to say to her
Saurabh: You don't need a speech. Just go
Akash: What if I say the wrong thing
Saurabh: Then say “I'm so sorry, I'm here.” That's plenty. Bring something to eat, and ask if you can take a small job, like the door or the tea
Akash: Ok. Five of us are going. Ravi wants to bring a big card for her to read later
Saurabh: Nice. Don't stay all day. Leave when she seems tired
Akash: Will do. Thank you
(Saturday night)
Akash: Went. Did the dishes, sat with her mother. Meera said, “Thanks for staying.” I said almost nothing. It was fine

qa.q: How many people were going to visit Meera?
qa.a: Five of them were going.

qa.q: What was Akash worried about before the visit?
qa.a: Akash was afraid of saying the wrong thing to Meera, since Akash did not know what to say.

qa.q: What did Akash do at Meera's home that mattered?
qa.a: Akash did the dishes, sat with Meera's mother and said very little, offering presence and a practical job rather than perfect words.

qa.q: What might the card from Ravi mean to Meera?
qa.a: Meera may find it comforting to read later, at her own pace, when she has room for it, since it shows the team cares without needing an answer.

grounding: An adult brings food, shows up, listens and offers practical help to a bereaved family, and presence is worth more than perfect words.

passage: When Ganpat kaka died suddenly in the fields, the whole village of Wadgaon crowded into his courtyard. People said the right words, touched Preeti kaki's feet and left. Vaibhav, who lived two houses down, didn't know what to say, so he didn't say much. He brought a pot of dal and rice every evening for a week. He milked their two buffaloes at dawn, since nobody else remembered them. When Preeti kaki wanted to talk about how Ganpat kaka hummed while tying his turban, Vaibhav sat on the step and listened, sometimes for an hour. On the tenth day she said, 'Everyone gave me advice. You gave me milk and dal and your ears.' Vaibhav looked down, embarrassed, and went to check the buffaloes.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav bring every evening for a week?
qa.a: A pot of dal and rice.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about not knowing what to say?
qa.a: He felt awkward and unsure with words, so he chose practical help instead.

qa.q: Which of Vaibhav's actions mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Milking the forgotten buffaloes and listening on the step; practical help and presence meant more than advice.

qa.q: How did Preeti kaki experience the villagers' visits compared with Vaibhav's help?
qa.a: The visits brought words and advice that didn't help much, while Vaibhav's food, work and listening made her feel truly supported.

grounding: A young man supports a bereaved neighbour through food, practical tasks and listening rather than perfect words.

passage: When Kofi's mother died, the whole office in Manchester signed a big card. Soo-ah signed it too, but it felt too small. She remembered that when her own grandmother died, what she had needed most was someone to take care of dinners. So she started a meal rota and asked eight colleagues to cover one evening each. She dropped off a pot of spiced rice with a note that just said, 'No need to reply.' At the funeral she didn't try to give a speech; she stood at the back and stacked chairs afterwards. Two weeks later, Kofi came back to work and stopped by her desk. 'I didn't eat properly for days. Then the food started arriving. Thank you.'

qa.q: How many colleagues did Soo-ah ask to join the meal rota?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: Why did the card feel too small to Soo-ah?
qa.a: She felt it wasn't enough, remembering that when her grandmother died she had most needed practical help with dinners.

qa.q: What made Soo-ah's help useful?
qa.a: Organising regular meals, adding a 'No need to reply' note, and helping quietly at the funeral instead of making speeches.

qa.q: How did the arriving food feel for Kofi?
qa.a: He hadn't been eating properly for days, so the meals likely felt like real care and relief.

grounding: A colleague supports a grieving co-worker with a meal rota and quiet presence rather than words.

passage: The morning after Naveen's father died, the badminton group at the community centre didn't play. Yash, who organised the Sunday games, made a list on the back of a score sheet: who could drive relatives from the station, who could bring tiffin, who could set up chairs for the prayer meeting. Nobody made a speech. Twelve names went down in twenty minutes. At the prayer meeting, Yash didn't try to find perfect words for Naveen. He just stood beside him while people came and went, and handed him water when his voice cracked. Later that week, when Naveen came back to the centre for the first time, the group played doubles as usual, and Yash made sure Naveen was on his side.

qa.q: What did Yash write the list on?
qa.a: The back of a score sheet.

qa.q: What might Naveen have felt when he came back and found the usual doubles game?
qa.a: Likely relieved and comforted, welcomed back to something normal without fuss.

qa.q: How did Yash turn the group's sympathy into real help?
qa.a: By listing practical tasks, like station pick-ups, tiffins and chairs, so twelve people could each do something useful.

qa.q: What was it like for the badminton group to be given specific tasks?
qa.a: They could act on their sadness instead of feeling helpless, which is why twelve names went down so quickly.

grounding: A community group supports a bereaved member through presence and practical tasks rather than perfect words.

passage:
Dear Manjula,
You asked what to say when you visit Farida's family next week. I learnt something this month, so let me tell you.
When Mr D'Souza downstairs died, I panicked about words. I rehearsed three sentences on the stairs and forgot all of them at the door. So I just held out the dal and rice. Mrs D'Souza took the dish and said, "Nobody has eaten since yesterday."
After that the colony found its jobs without any meeting. Rafiq uncle handled the chairs. The Nair girls took the grandchildren to the park. I came every evening at seven to wash the steel glasses and sit in a corner. Some evenings nobody spoke to me at all.
Last Sunday she held my wrist and said, "You came every day." Not one word about anything I'd said.
So go, Manju. Take something. Stay a while.
Your akka,
Chandrika

qa.q: What did Chandrika bring to the D'Souza home?
qa.a: Chandrika held out the dal and rice.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel at the door the first time?
qa.a: She was nervous and panicky about saying the right thing, and forgot all three sentences she had rehearsed.

qa.q: What does Chandrika advise Manjula, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To go, take something and stay a while, because being present and doing small tasks mattered more to Mrs D'Souza than perfect words.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza experience Chandrika's evening visits?
qa.a: She felt cared for by the steady presence; what she remembered was "You came every day", not anything that was said.

grounding: Chandrika's letter shows an adult supporting a bereaved family with food, presence and small tasks rather than perfect words.
